title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
This incident shows impersonation at scale through synthetic media. Criminals used AI-generated videos to create hundreds of fake social media accounts impersonating a real immigration attorney, then directed vulnerable immigrants to pay for fraudulent legal services through digital payment apps. The scam exploited both the trust immigrants place in established legal professionals and the difficulty of verifying authenticity on social media platforms.

The failure occurred at the point of initial contact. Social media platforms did not prevent the creation and proliferation of fake accounts using synthetic video before they caused financial harm. An anti-piracy company eventually removed thousands of accounts, but this was reactive rather than preventive. Detection would have required either platform-based screening of video content and account authenticity before accounts could operate, or verification mechanisms that immigrants could use to confirm they were contacting a real attorney.

It is not established whether the social media platforms were aware of the accounts before removal, what technical measures they had deployed to prevent synthetic impersonation, or how the scammers initially created and scaled the fake profiles.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become a victim of artificial intelligence fraud targeting vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake social media profiles and AI-generated videos featuring Leal, falsely advertising immigration services such as US residency assistance for $2,200. The scams escalated dramatically over the past three months after potential clients began calling his office. An anti-piracy company hired by Leal's firm has removed nearly 6,500 fake accounts, including 3,500 on TikTok, 2,400 on Facebook, and 544 on Instagram.

The fraudulent scheme typically starts with social media videos directing viewers to contact a WhatsApp number, where scammers send phony contracts and request payment through apps like Venmo, Zelle, or Cash App. Some fake videos include testimonials from supposed former clients praising Leal for securing legal status. Leal warns immigrants to verify the identity of legal service providers online and avoid anyone requesting immediate payment through digital payment apps. He has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the scams' origin.
